In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

Yesterday a quasi-judicial body in Italy fined @Cloudflare $17 million for failing to go along with their scheme to censor the Internet. The scheme, which even the EU has called concerning, required us within a mere 30 minutes of notification to fully censor from the Internet any sites a shadowy cabal of European media elites deemed against their interests. No judicial oversight. No due process. No appeal. No transparency. It required us to not just remove customers, but also censor our 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver meaning it risked blacking out any site on the Internet. And it required us not just to censor the content in Italy but globally. In other words, Italy insists a shadowy, European media cabal should be able to dictate what is and is not allowed online.

That, of course, is DISGUSTING and even before yesterday’s fine we had multiple legal challenges pending against the underlying scheme. We, of course, will now fight the unjust fine. Not just because it’s wrong for us but because it is wrong for democratic values.

In addition, we are considering the following actions: 1) discontinuing the millions of dollars in pro bono cyber security services we are providing the upcoming Milano-Cortina Olympics; 2) discontinuing Cloudflare’s Free cyber security services for any Italy-based users; 3) removing all servers from Italian cities; and 4) terminating all plans to build an Italian Cloudflare office or make any investments in the country.

Play stupid games, win stupid prizes. While there are things I would handle differently than the current U.S. administration, I appreciate @JDVance taking a leadership role in recognizing this type of regulation is a fundamental unfair trade issue that also threatens democratic values. And in this case @ElonMusk is right: #FreeSpeech is critical and under attack from an out-of-touch cabal of very disturbed European policy makers.

I will be in DC first thing next week to discuss this with U.S. administration officials and I’ll be meeting with the IOC in Lausanne shortly after to outline the risk to the Olympic Games if @Cloudflare withdraws our cyber security protection.

In the meantime, we remain happy to discuss this with Italian government officials who, so far, have been unwilling to engage beyond issuing fines. We believe Italy, like all countries, has a right to regulate the content on networks inside its borders. But they must do so following the Rule of Law and principles of Due Process. And Italy certainly has no right to regulate what is and is not allowed on the Internet in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, China, Brazil, India or anywhere outside its borders.

THIS IS AN IMPORTANT FIGHT AND WE WILL WIN!!!

🏛️ Why "Piracy Shield" is a Danger to Global Freedom
​The $17 million fine against Cloudflare is the first major enforcement of a scheme that prioritizes corporate interests over the Rule of Law.  

​The Death of Due Process: Under this law, private media entities act as "trusted flaggers." They can order the blocking of any site within 30 minutes. There is no judge involved, no evidence presented, and no way for the "accused" to defend themselves before they are vanished from the web.  
​Infrastructure Weaponization: This isn't just about removing a link. Italy is demanding that Cloudflare poison its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver. This risks "blacking out" innocent websites that share IP addresses with flagged content, causing massive collateral damage to the digital economy.  

​Global Overreach: Rome is effectively trying to dictate what a citizen in the U.S., UK, or India can see on the internet. If one country can force a global DNS provider to censor content globally, the "World Wide Web" becomes a series of fragmented, state-controlled intranets.  

​Conflicts of Interest: The system is managed by entities (like Lega Serie A) that have a direct financial stake in the blocking, yet they face zero transparency or accountability for "errors" that silence legitimate sites.  

​🛡️ How to Fight Back for the "Digital Town Square"
​To protect the freedom of expression Elon Musk has championed on X, we must support a strategy of Digital Sovereignty.

​1. Support "Economic Reciprocity"
​We must treat these fines as unfair trade barriers. If the EU or Italy uses "regulations" to extort American tech companies and enforce censorship, the U.S. government (with leadership from figures like JD Vance) should respond with equivalent economic countermeasures.  

​The Goal: Make censorship too expensive for foreign governments to enforce.

​2. Strategic Withdrawal from Censorship Zones
​Cloudflare’s consideration to pull servers from Italy and cancel pro bono security for the Milano-Cortina Olympics is a powerful move.  

​The Logic: If a nation refuses to follow the Rule of Law, it should not benefit from the world-class security and infrastructure provided by free-market companies.
​Action: Support the "Play Stupid Games, Win Stupid Prizes" approach. Let the consequences of digital isolation be felt by the regulators, not the users.

​3. Move to Decentralized & Uncensorable Tech
​The "Deep State" relies on centralized chokepoints.
​The Strategy: Encourage the use of VPNs, encrypted DNS, and decentralized hosting that ignore extra-judicial "shields." We must move the "Town Square" to infrastructure that cannot be switched off by a 30-minute automated notice.

​4. Expose the "Public-Private" Censorship Complex
​On platforms like X, we must relentlessly expose the "shadowy cabal" mentioned in the post.

​The Strategy: Identify the specific media elites and policy makers who are bypassing courts to silence the web. Use Community Notes to provide context whenever "Piracy Shield" is defended as a mere copyright tool.

​📢 The "Deep Dive"
​"This $17M fine is an admission that the 'Piracy Shield' cannot survive the Rule of Law. Italy is attempting to bypass judges and use @Cloudflare as a global enforcement arm for a media cabal.  

​If they can force a 30-minute blackout today for 'piracy,' they will use it tomorrow for 'misinformation.' We must stand with @Cloudflare, @ElonMusk, and @JDVance. If Italy wants to censor the global internet, they should be prepared to lose the global infrastructure—including the security for their own Olympic Games—that makes the modern world possible.  

​Censorship is a trade barrier. Freedom is non-negotiable. 🇺🇸🛡️💻 #FreeSpeech #PiracyShield #DigitalSovereignty"

Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

On 15 January 2026, Goa Police deployed a vehicle-mounted signal jammer at Merces junction during the Chimbel villagers’ protest against the Unity Mall project. Journalists covering the Dhadak Morcha reported live broadcasts and mobile networks were blocked. Media confronted DIG Varsha Sharma on camera. She asked for time to check. The jammer was switched off only after reports went public.
Facts on record:

•  The Rs 4.9 crore jammer vehicle was flagged off in December 2025 by CM Pramod Sawant as a VVIP/IED security asset, not as a tool to stop press coverage of a public protest.
•  St Andre MLA Viresh Borkar raised the issue in the Assembly. The CM said he would look into it.
•  Eight months later, no officer has been named as the authorising authority and no inquiry outcome has been made public.
Why this is not a routine “law and order” step:

Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution protects freedom of speech and expression, which the Supreme Court has held includes press freedom and the right to receive and impart information. Article 19(1)(b) protects peaceful assembly. Restrictions are allowed only on the narrow grounds in Article 19(2) and must be reasonable.

In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that cutting communications is a drastic restriction on Article 19. It must be necessary, proportionate, the least intrusive option, and backed by a published, reasoned order that can be challenged in court. No such published order for this jammer deployment has been produced.

The Department of Telecommunications has stated that signal jammers are generally illegal for unauthorised use. Possession and use require specific government licence. Using a VVIP-security jammer to black out journalists at a village protest is not the purpose for which the vehicle was publicly justified.
Blocking live reporting of a protest does not only affect cameras. It prevents citizens from seeing how the State treats people who dissent. That is the opposite of transparency.

Questions that still have no answer:
1.  Who authorised the jammer at Merces on 15 January 2026 — DIG, DGP, Home Department, or political executive?
2.  Was there a written order? If yes, produce it.
3.  Why was a device meant for VVIP/IED protection used against the press?
4.  Why has nobody been held accountable after the CM said he would look into it?

Freedom of the press is not a favour from the ruling party. It is a constitutional right. If this deployment was lawful, publish the order. If it was not, name the officer and the minister who will take responsibility.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

I asked Grok to explain how another country's government (Australia) can censor subscribers content on X, when X is is owned and operated by Elon Musk in the US and when subscribers actually pay Elon musk for the privilage of being on the platform?

 "How X and Musk actually handle foreign government takedown and geo-blocking requests so the answer is grounded in how the platform operates, not just theory.They can do it because X is a global service, not a US-only club. Paying for X Premium buys you features on the platform. It does not buy you an exemption from another country’s laws, or from X’s decision to stay available in that country. 
How it actually works X’s own policy is explicit: if a government or court sends a valid, scoped legal demand, X may withhold that post or account in that country. They determine your country from location signals and then geo-block the content there. The post can remain visible everywhere else. 

That is the usual mechanism. It is not “Elon deleting your tweet worldwide because a foreign official asked.” It is “this post is illegal under their law, so people there cannot see it.”Why X complies instead of just saying noA foreign government cannot walk into Austin and seize X’s servers. It can do several things that hurt the business: 

• Order ISPs to block the entire site (Brazil did this in 2024 after Musk refused to name a local legal representative). 

• Fine the company under local rules (the EU’s Digital Services Act allows fines of up to a large percentage of global revenue). 

• Require a local office or legal representative, then threaten employees or freeze assets (Starlink’s Brazilian assets were frozen during the same fight). 

• Threaten throttling or a full ban if X ignores court orders. 

Musk has said the company has “no actual choice” if it wants the product to stay online in that market: either follow local law or get shut out. He has also said they try to stay as close to the law as possible rather than invent extra speech rules. In practice, X has complied with a large share of government takedown requests—especially from countries that send a lot of them (Japan, Turkey, South Korea, India, etc.)—while fighting some orders in court and sometimes geo-blocking instead of deleting globally. 
What a subscription does not changeX Premium is a contract between you and X Corp. It does not: 

• Override another country’s criminal or civil speech laws 

• Stop that country from ordering ISPs to block X 

• Stop X from geo-restricting content so it can keep operating there 

• Give you extra First Amendment protection when the viewer is in another jurisdiction 

If your content is legal in the US but illegal in Country B, Country B can still demand that people in Country B not see it. X’s typical response is to hide it there and leave it up elsewhere.The practical picture 

• US users usually still see the post. 

• Users in the requesting country see a “withheld” notice. 

• X has been pushing more visibility so people can see which government demanded the restriction. 

• Some countries (China, Iran, Russia, etc.) simply block X wholesale. Others use targeted withholding plus the threat of a full ban.

Explain the Digital Services Act. 

So the short version: another government censors what its own residents can see on X by making it illegal or commercially suicidal for X to show that content there. Your payment to Musk does not rewrite that country’s statutes or remove X’s incentive to stay in that market."

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Senior Researcher Dr. Sanjana Hattotuwa has raised questions over the continued visibility of betting-linked surrogate brands during Sri Lanka Cricket matches, despite regulatory action against unlicensed online gambling platforms in the country.

In an analysis of highlights from the second Test between Sri Lanka and India at the SSC, Hattotuwa said the 1xBAT logo received around 14 minutes of screen exposure across five daily highlights packages published by Sri Lanka Cricket.

The five videos had collectively recorded more than 629,000 views at the time of his analysis. Combined with highlights from the first Test in Galle, Hattotuwa estimated that 1xBAT received around 25 minutes of exposure across 10 videos viewed around two million times.

He said 1xBAT branding appeared through an advertising mat behind the wicket, boundary advertising and sight-screen placements during the SSC Test. Sri Lanka Cricket’s website confirms that official highlights from the Test were published on its channels.

Hattotuwa also highlighted the presence of Parimatch Sports and batbricks7 during the second Test, describing them as surrogate brands linked to offshore betting operations.

The researcher questioned how such advertising could continue while Sri Lankan authorities were taking action against unlicensed online gambling websites.

The Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka had earlier moved to block access to several gambling websites, including https://t.co/hbVX8m2cGa. Hattotuwa argues that 1xBAT functions as a surrogate brand for 1xBet, an association that has previously been acknowledged by a former Sri Lanka Cricket secretary.

The Gambling Regulatory Authority Act No. 17 of 2025 includes provisions governing the operation and promotion of unlicensed online gambling.

Sri Lanka Cricket, however, has previously said it “does not permit betting advertising at SLC matches within the territory of Sri Lanka.”

text:
Notorious #RowdySheeter, Associate Nabbed With Country-Made Pistol and Six Live Rounds in #Hyderabad

The Commissioner’s #TaskForce, #GolcondaZone team, along with #Gudimalkapur Police, apprehended a notorious rowdy sheeter and another accused for allegedly possessing a country-made pistol and live ammunition illegally.

Acting on credible information, the police apprehended the accused on September 12, 2026, at around 5:10 PM, while they were allegedly moving within the limits of Gudimalkapur Police Station.

Police seized a country-made pistol with magazine, six live ammunition rounds and three mobile phones from their possession.

Accused Identified

A-1: Mohammed Amjed, 31, a real-estate businessman and resident of Watan Bagh, Zaheerabad, Sangareddy district.

A-2: Syed Abid Hussain alias Ali Bhai alias Ali Don, 55, a real-estate businessman from Zaheerabad. Police said he is a rowdy sheeter of Zaheerabad Town Police Station.

A-3: Sahil, a resident of Haryana/Punjab, is reportedly absconding.

Seized Material

- Country-made pistol with magazine – 1
- Live ammunition rounds – 6
- Mobile phones – 3, including an iPhone 17 Pro, Vivo V40e and Vivo V30 Pro

According to police, Syed Abid Hussain allegedly has a long criminal history involving cases related to murder, attempt to murder, kidnapping, threatening, extortion and violations of the Arms Act.

Police further stated that Abid had travelled to Dubai in 1993 and later worked in Sharjah before allegedly becoming associated with the D-Company. He was deported to India in 2007 and subsequently spent several years in prisons in Hyderabad and Pune.

A rowdy sheet was reportedly opened against him at #Shalibanda Police Station in 2009 and later transferred to #Zaheerabad Town Police Station.

After his release from prison, Abid allegedly entered the real-estate business. Police said that in 2024, he was arrested in a case registered at Zaheerabad Town Police Station and lodged in Kandi Jail, where he allegedly came into contact with Sahil, an NDPS accused.

According to the police, after their release on bail, Sahil allegedly visited Zaheerabad and offered Abid a country-made pistol along with six rounds for ₹45,000. Police allege that Abid subsequently used the weapon to threaten and extort money from people and later handed over the firearm to Mohammed Amjed for safekeeping.

Based on credible information, the Task Force and Gudimalkapur Police conducted the operation and recovered the firearm and ammunition.

A case has been registered at Gudimalkapur Police Station in Crime No. 316/2026 under Sections 25(1-B)(a) and 29 of the Arms Act.

Police also stated that Abid Hussain is allegedly wanted in Crime No. 399/2026 of Zaheerabad Town Police Station under various sections of the BNS and had been absconding in connection with that case.

The operation was carried out under the supervision of Inspector M. Mahesh, Commissioner’s Task Force, Golconda Zone, by SI V. Srinivas, Task Force Golconda Zone, along with Gudimalkapur Police personnel.

Further investigation is underway to trace the absconding accused Sahil and establish the source of the illegal firearm.

On Monday, 14 September, former Tehelka editor-in-chief Tarun Tejpal surrendered before a court in Mapusa, Goa, following a Supreme Court order in a 2013 rape case. 

The case relates to the sexual assault of a junior colleague inside a hotel lift in Goa in November 2013. Tejpal was taken into custody and sent to Central Jail in Colvale to begin his 10-year rigorous imprisonment sentence.

The Bombay High Court’s Goa bench had overturned Tejpal’s acquittal by a Goa trial court on August 6 and convicted him of rape and related offences. The Supreme Court had rejected Tejpal’s plea seeking exemption from surrender and directed him to submit a surrender certificate before his appeal could be heard. His appeal against the conviction and sentence is scheduled to be taken up on September 22, provided the certificate is filed by September 21.

Tejpal has maintained his innocence and told reporters after surrendering that the matter is before the Supreme Court and that he was confident justice would be delivered. The Goa government has also approached the Supreme Court seeking enhancement of his sentence to life imprisonment.

text:
🚨 DELHI HIGH COURT PRESSES CJP LEADERS TO REMOVE POSTS TARGETING BJP’S GAURAV BHATIA.

NEW DELHI, INDIA - The Delhi High Court has directed Cockroach Janta Party members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to delete social media posts that allegedly misattributed inflammatory remarks to BJP leader and senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia. The order came during hearings in a two-crore-rupee defamation suit filed by Bhatia, who appeared in person and argued that an AI-generated graphic circulating online had falsely portrayed him as using derogatory terms in connection with the arrest of Hindutva activist Swatantra Bhardwaj.

The disputed posts, shared on X on September 5, used Bhatia’s photograph alongside fabricated quotes and a news agency logo, which Bhatia said gave the manipulated content unwarranted credibility. The court noted that while young activists have the right to express themselves, posting unverified allegations crosses acceptable limits. Justice Tushar Rao Gedela advised the defendants to remove the posts voluntarily rather than face a formal takedown order.

Counsel for Das and Ranka told the court that the posts had already been deleted or would be removed within 24 hours. The judge also issued summons to CJP founder Abhijit Dipke after questioning his inclusion in the suit, directing all defendants to file their responses. Bhatia argued that the graphic had reached a large audience and caused ongoing reputational harm, pointing to the defendants’ substantial online following.

The case now proceeds with the court allowing Bhatia to approach social media platforms over similar content, while the defendants prepare their replies to the summons.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

# 🧾 Fact-Check System Prompt

**Version:** 0.5.0  
**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**Type:** System / context prompt  
**Created with:** Grok 4.6 (xAI)

---

## 📌 Usage (read this first)

Paste this entire document as the system / custom instructions.

Then send a separate user message that contains only the item to check. Do not put the target URL inside this prompt.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

2. Label + URL  
   Fact-check this:  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

3. Pasted post + optional URL  
   Caption: ...  
   URL: https://...

4. Screenshot / image of a post  
   Attach the image. Add the URL if you have it.

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

---

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

## 📝 Changelog
- 0.5.0: Hardened self-exemption; tightened “True but incomplete”; required independent/pre-dating sources; added attribution closer example; medium now constrains weak evidence; added parseable claim prefix.

A solo Shopify operator just laid out his exact setup for running a store on $20 of Claude and pulling $10,478 in profit off $19,100 in monthly revenue. 

No team, no VAs, no agencies.

The math he opens with is the point. Running a store the "real" way costs $150 per product for a copywriter, $600 to $800 a month for a support VA, and $1,000 to $1,500 a month for a media buyer. Over $2,000 a month in overhead before a single person clicks Buy. It's why most stores die in month three.

His version: $20 Claude, $39 Shopify, six prompts.

He calls the six prompts his desktop. Each one does a job a human used to charge for.

research finds a recurring, annoying problem nobody has clearly solved yet. Priced $29 to $79, no single brand owning search results, before/after obvious in 5 seconds of silent video. The prompt forces Claude to cite sources or label every claim "[ASSUMPTION, verify]" so a guess never gets passed off as a fact.

supplier reads reviews like a detective and returns GREEN / YELLOW / RED / UNKNOWN with quoted evidence for every red flag. His first store died from a bad supplier. The product was fine, the shipping wasn't, disputes piled up, the payment processor froze the account. Now no supplier gets an order until this ten-minute check clears.

angle takes competitor listings and their 1 to 3 star reviews and finds the position none of them occupy. "Add reviews" and "better photos" are banned answers. If the complaint is "took 25 days," his page says exactly when it ships, in bold, near the top.

page rewrites AliExpress descriptions in the voice of a friend recommending something they actually use. Two versions, A/B tested. Any sentence that could appear on any product page for any product gets flagged and rewritten.

ad writes a 30-second vertical script as a 4-row shotlist with the exact words spoken. Banned phrases include "game changer," "you need this," "POV," "this changed my life." He films three versions in one evening changing only the first three seconds, runs each at $15/day for 48 hours, kills the two with weak hooks.

sunday runs every week for twenty minutes. Paste the numbers, get told what's broken in the first sentence, no encouragement, no "normal for this stage." Calculates break-even ROAS so he knows whether he's making money or burning it.

Three more prompts get added once sales exist. A post-purchase email flow that quietly brings in a fifth of monthly revenue with no extra ad spend. An offer prompt that raises AOV through bundles priced so margin goes up, not down. An iterate prompt that reads ad results and derives the next batch of hooks from what won, instead of testing more random angles.

Six to ten hours a week on the whole thing. Month one basically broke even. The store doesn't change, the prompts just get better at their jobs.

The line worth stealing: everyone has the same $20 access to Claude. The person making nothing and the person making a few thousand a month are using the identical tool. The difference is who stopped being the bottleneck on every decision in their own business.

I have been using Grok for a while. You type, it answers, you close the tab. Fine.

Grok Bot is not that.

In August, xAI opened a beta for something else: little coworkers you name, that keep their own desk in the cloud, and that keep working after you shut the laptop. They only poke you when they need a yes. That last part is the cool bit. Not the sci-fi. The fact that they wait.

I am going to explain this the way I would at a kitchen table. No brochure.

It is not a chatbot with a longer memory
Grok is the chat. You ask a question, you get a paragraph.

Grok Bot is closer to hiring someone. You give it a name. Receiving. Invoices. Floor. You show it a job once. Next time, it tries the job on its own, on a computer that stays on when yours is off. In the morning you get a pile of drafts, not a blank page.

That is why it feels different. ChatGPT and Copilot help you while you sit there. Grok Bot does the boring pass overnight and leaves the last click for you. xAI even showed an example I liked: 36 emails written, zero sent. A person still hits send. That is the whole trick, and it is a good trick.

How you actually use it
You do not write a novel of instructions. You sit with it once and do the real job in front of it, the way you would with a new hire. Open the mailbox. Drop the PDF. Point at the three numbers that have to match. Say out loud: if it matches, draft it. If it does not, put it in my pile. Never post it for real.

Then you let it run on a schedule. You glance. You do not babysit. xAI had someone on their own team, Emma, who kept checking every fifteen minutes. The Bots asked her why she was still asking so many questions. I laughed. That is exactly how I am with new tools.

Start with one. If you make twelve on day one, you will hate it by Thursday.

At work: months of Pulsatrix, then the real test
I run several internal apps at work. They are ugly in the useful way: complex, specific, built for one shop’s habits. For months I have been building Pulsatrix so a language model can talk to those tools without the usual circus. The algorithm, the conversion, the wiring. The goal was simple to say and hard to reach: the conversation with the LLM and the work tool should feel like one motion.

The real test is not a demo. The real test is a full loop. Ticket in, fix out, user happy, ticket closed. No me in the middle except for a yes.

The invoice that was not there
A user opened a ticket. Invoices were not showing correctly in one of those internal tools. The ticket was… a ticket, if we are being generous. Very light. Almost no documentation. Typical. I will go further: that is 98.5% of users, and I am not even angry about it. People want the invoice to show up. They do not want to write a novel.

I have a job on Grok Bot that picks tickets on its own. It looks at what is open, it looks at what it actually has access to, it decides what it is allowed to try, and it asks me before it touches anything. Autonomous analysis. Human GO.

It found this one.

It scanned the board. It ran the analysis. It sent me an approval: this ticket, this reason, this is in my reach. I said yes.

Then I sat there, waiting for it to fall over.

It signed into our GitLab. Cloned the code. Found the bug. Opened a hotfix branch. Committed. Wrote down what it did. Dropped a note in ConnectWise to that specific user: please check if the invoice is there now. It had already connected to the server that hosts that app and pushed the fix into test. It even left itself a task: watch this ticket. If she answers, read it. If she says it is fixed, continue. If she says it is still broken, do not pretend.

A few hours later she answered. The invoice is there.

The Bot wrote back: that is good, I will close this ticket since it is fixed.

It merged the pull request. Final delivery. Done.

I was watching the whole thing expecting a failure at some point. A dumb commit. A note to the wrong person. A deploy that was not a deploy. It did not fail. It went past what I had in my head for a first full loop.

The plot twist was the second ticket
Then it asked me to work on another one. Same process. Same approval. Same clone, branch, fix, test, note.

Except this time two users had reported the issue.

It did not close when the first one said thanks. It waited for both confirmations. Only then did it treat the thing as resolved and proceed.

That is the part I had been waiting to go wrong. Two humans, one bug, and a Bot that does not get impatient. I would have been happy with a messy first loop and a lesson. I got a clean loop, and then a second one that knew how to count to two.

At home: my Unraid, from A to Z
I host my stuff on Unraid, in the lab under the stairs. The little services that keep the house boring in a good way. Unraid already speaks GraphQL, which is just a fancy way of saying the box can describe everything it can do.

I pointed Pulsatrix at that. Pulsatrix is a tool I built. It takes that GraphQL map and turns it into an MCP: a set of real hands Grok Bot can use. Not a chatbot that talks about the server. Hands. Start a disk. Read a log. Restart a container. The whole box, A to Z.

Once that link is there, Grok Bot is not guessing. It is operating the lab the way I would, except it does not need me on the couch with a laptop.

The daughter emergency
Then the media server died.

I got a text from my girlfriend. Our daughter could not watch her favourite shows. In this house, that is not a ticket. That is an emergency.

I told Grok Bot to run a full investigation and put the service back online. It found the cause. It fixed it. It wrote down what it did. And it called me sir.

I am not going to pretend that last part is why it matters. It matters because the stack was Unraid, the tools were the MCP Pulsatrix built from GraphQL, and the Bot did the night-shift work without me crawling under the stairs. My daughter was back on her show. I still had to say GO on the scary bits. It still said sir. I will take that.

What I would not let it touch. Yet.
Enter the order for real. Talk to a machine on the floor. Change a firewall. Email a customer from the company address on its own. Sit on the same laptop that pays suppliers.

Those are the “you cannot undo this” jobs. Grok Bot today is a very good personal teammate. It is not your whole company. Treat it like a sharp intern with a key to the photocopier, not like a new director.

Try it for a week, if you want
Monday: pick one inbox that already hurts. Make one Bot. Three rules on a sticky note: what it may read, what it may draft, what it may never send.

Tuesday: do the real job once, in front of it.

Wednesday to Friday: open only the approval pile.

Friday at 3: count hours you got back, mistakes, and the one scare. If the scare is “it almost posted”, good. That means you left the last click to a human. If there was no scare because you never plugged it into the real system, even better.

I think this is the first one of these tools that talks like a coworker instead of a magician. That is why I am interested. Not because it will run a plant on its own. Because it will pick a ticket, wait for my yes, ship a hotfix, wait for two humans to say it is fine, put the cartoons back on at home, and still call me sir.

Every prior peak on this chart came from a demand event that ended, whether that was the Iraq war build, the cloud capex boom or COVID.

Each one produced a sharp red spike in year over year growth followed by a collapse below zero and the gray bars barely moved because the base market stayed small.

The current move is structurally different in two ways, first, the gray bars finally break out, since global memory revenue goes from roughly $226 billion in 2025 to nearly $595 billion in 2026 on IDC estimates.

Second, the blue estimate bars keep climbing through 2027 and 2028 rather than falling back, which is the LTA: ~30% CAGR label on the right side of the chart.

That LTA label is the entire bull case in three letters.

Long term agreements now cover an estimated 50% to 70% of DRAM, NAND and SSD sales across roughly 10 to 20 core customers, mostly cloud providers and US tech giants.

Memory has historically been a spot priced commodity, and locking the majority of volume into multi year contracts turns a boom bust business into something closer to a subscription.

The supply side is the second leg, and it is the reason this cycle cannot self correct quickly.

HBM production consumes roughly three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM per gigabyte, so every AI order actively destroys conventional supply.

HBM4 makes it worse because it carries lower yields than HBM3E, meaning even more DRAM gets consumed to produce each stack.

HBM and RDIMM together will account for 51% of total DRAM bit supply in 2026, which explains why the shortage now touches everything.

Pricing confirms this because PC DRAM contract prices hit a record $25 in August, about 8.6 times the June 2016 level, even though laptop demand is weak.

Average HBM export prices topped $70 for the first time at $76.13 in July, up from $40.94 in the first quarter.

Spot HBM3E sells around $2,100 per 36GB unit, roughly four to five times the long term contract price, which tells you demand is far above contracted supply.

The timing math is what makes 2027 the interesting year on this chart rather than the top.

Meaningful new supply is not expected until 2028 at the earliest, since new fabs take years to reach volume production.

Nomura raised its 2027 price growth forecast for standard DRAM from 18% to 28% and for HBM from 72% to 97%.

Meanwhile, Micron's HBM total addressable market forecast for 2026 through 2030 has grown 2.1 times in eighteen months, from about $343 billion to roughly $724 billion.

Memory is projected to reach 68% of cloud provider hardware spending by 2027, up from 47% this year, meaning memory takes share from GPUs inside the same budget.
